enrichment.short_title: Child sexual abuse convictions quashed after post-trial interview revealed complainant had named many more alleged abusers than at trial
key_facts: Bond, Frost-Smith and Cook were convicted in 1996 at Maidstone of sexual offences against two girls, J and C; medical evidence confirmed prolonged abuse but individual attribution was disputed.

Following conviction, J gave a post-trial interview naming about 18 further alleged abusers, including her mother as a participant, materially inconsistent with her pre-trial accounts in which she said she had told all.
The Criminal Cases Review Commission referred Bond's conviction; Frost-Smith and Cook then applied for leave to appeal on the same credibility grounds.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal against conviction following CCRC referral (Bond) and renewed leave applications (Frost-Smith and Cook) in the Court of Appeal (Criminal Division).
enrichment.outcome: Appeals allowed; convictions set aside as unsafe; retrial refused given time already served.
enrichment.ratio: Where a principal complainant's post-trial disclosures would have afforded the defence substantial material to challenge her credibility and suggest confabulation or mistaken identification of peripheral defendants, convictions are unsafe if that material was not before the jury.
legal_issues: Whether post-trial allegations undermining J's credibility rendered the 1996 convictions unsafe
Whether the Crown could distinguish between appellants when CCRC reasons related primarily to Bond
Whether retrial was appropriate after lengthy imprisonment already served

enrichment.short_title: Gypsy family's challenge to refusal of permanent mobile homes at Brent Knoll dismissed on all five planning grounds
key_facts: Mrs Jones, a gypsy, sought planning permission for three permanent mobile homes at Oakdale, Brent Knoll, Somerset, for herself, her daughter's family and her elderly mother.
An Inspector dismissed her appeal, finding harm to the countryside setting of Brent Knoll and insufficient special circumstances to outweigh landscape policies.
The site lies within a Special Landscape Feature area subject to strict development control; Shane's special educational needs were likely to be met in Bridgwater, some distance away.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Application for judicial review of an Inspector's decision dismissing a planning appeal; permission to appeal refused.
enrichment.outcome: Application dismissed on all five grounds; costs ordered against the applicant subject to public funding provisions.
enrichment.ratio: An Inspector who addresses general gypsy site provision alongside personal circumstances, evaluates material considerations discretely but reaches an overall balanced conclusion, and properly applies Circular 11/95 on temporary permissions has not erred in law; Article 8 interference was proportionate to environmental protection.
legal_issues: Whether the Inspector failed to consider general unmet gypsy site need
Whether material considerations in favour of permission were assessed cumulatively
Whether temporary planning permission should have been granted
Whether Circular 1/94 'other protected areas' was misapplied against local plan policy H34
Whether educational needs of Shane were properly weighed against site distance from Bridgwater

notes: Complete boundary dispute appeal with conveyancing and estoppel analysis.

enrichment.short_title: Misplaced boundary fence at Rolle Barton development; conveyance plan prevails over erroneous physical features and proprietary estoppel fails
key_facts: Countrywide Properties converted farm buildings at Rolle Barton, Otterton into three residential plots; Mrs Harvey bought Plot 1 (Phoenix Barn) and the Beales later bought Plot 2 (The Shippen).
A post-and-wire fence and retaining wall were erected south of the plan boundary, giving Mrs Harvey about 50 sq metres of disputed garden land which she landscaped before the Beales' purchase.
The Recorder granted a mandatory injunction requiring realignment of the fence along the straight plan line; Mrs Harvey's estoppel defence was rejected at trial for inadequate pleading.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal from Exeter County Court (Recorder Lambert) following refusal of summary judgment and full trial on boundary and estoppel issues.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; true boundary follows the conveyance plan line; proprietary estoppel defence rejected on the merits.
enrichment.ratio: Where land is conveyed by reference to a plan, the red-edged boundary line on the plan is the dominant description and an erroneously placed fence or wall does not alter the true boundary; proprietary estoppel requires unconscionable repudiation and insubstantial detriment will not suffice where the developer offered to rectify its mistake at its own expense.
legal_issues: Construction of parcels clauses and annexed plans in transfers
Whether physical features on the ground at completion override plan boundaries
Admissibility of subsequent conduct to resolve latent ambiguity
Whether equitable/proprietary estoppel was adequately pleaded and made out

enrichment.short_title: Common law public nuisance held compatible with Convention rights; Goldstein's salt-in-envelope anthrax scare conviction upheld
key_facts: Two appeals raised whether the common law offence of public nuisance survived the Human Rights Act 1998 and was sufficiently certain under Article 7.
R faced a preliminary ruling on an indictment for sending 538 postal packages containing racially offensive material over nine years; Leveson J held public nuisance was a known offence.
Goldstein posted an envelope containing salt to a supplier during the post-9/11 anthrax scare; salt leaked at Wembley sorting office causing evacuation of 110 workers.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Joint Court of Appeal hearing: R appealed a preliminary ruling under CPIA 1996; Goldstein appealed against conviction.
enrichment.outcome: Both appeals dismissed; public nuisance held valid and Convention-compatible; questions certified for House of Lords but leave refused.
enrichment.ratio: Public nuisance remains a known common law offence with sufficient legal certainty under Article 7; its flexible definition is a proportionate interference with Articles 8 and 10 where conduct materially affects public comfort or safety; cumulative campaigns of harassment may constitute a single public nuisance.
legal_issues: Whether public nuisance is too vague to survive as a common law offence
Compatibility with Articles 7, 8 and 10 ECHR
Whether R's 538 letters could be tried as one public nuisance
Whether Goldstein's act was 'not warranted by law' and required intent to simulate anthrax
Mens rea under R v Shorrock

enrichment.short_title: Permission to appeal refused over time-barred equal pay and wages claims against Rhône-Poulenc
key_facts: Mrs Amica brought equal pay, wages and Article 119 Treaty of Rome claims against Rhône-Poulenc Chemicals Ltd relating to employment ending 31 December 1993.
The Manchester Employment Tribunal found all claims out of time; she alleged delay caused by a withheld 1977 equal pay memorandum, workplace harassment and ill health.
The EAT dismissed her appeal, relying on Preston v Wolverhampton Health Authority; she also challenged EAT orders about disclosure of the 1977 memorandum.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Applications for permission to appeal to the Court of Appeal from multiple EAT orders, principally the dismissal of her appeal from the Employment Tribunal.
enrichment.outcome: All applications for permission to appeal refused.
enrichment.ratio: Where an Employment Tribunal properly finds equal pay and Article 119 claims out of time and a wages claim not reasonably practicable to bring in time, subsequent House of Lords authority in Preston does not revive the claim; a 1977 memorandum could not alter that time-bar conclusion.
legal_issues: Whether equal pay and Article 119 claims were brought in time
Effect of Preston on Community law equal pay claims
Relevance of a withheld 1977 equal pay memorandum
Whether EAT disclosure orders were reversible

enrichment.short_title: Court guidance on when NHS trusts must seek High Court approval before terminating pregnancy of mentally incapacitated woman
key_facts: D, an 18-year-old with severe schizophrenia detained under the Mental Health Act 1983, was found pregnant; two doctors certified termination was necessary to prevent grave permanent injury to her mental health.
Coleridge J had earlier granted a declaration that termination was in D's best interests ([2002] EWHC (Fam) 3189).
The parties sought wider guidance on whether court authorisation is always required where a patient lacks capacity to consent to abortion.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Supplementary judgment following adjournment for further submissions on the general need for declaratory relief in incapacitated-patient abortion cases.
enrichment.outcome: Guidance given: court application not required where capacity and best interests are clear and uncontested, but required where there is dispute, lack of unanimity, Abortion Act non-compliance, family opposition, or other exceptional circumstances.
enrichment.ratio: Abortion Act certification adequately protects competent patients but not incapacitated women who cannot decide for themselves; under Article 8 the court should authorise termination where capacity or best interests are doubtful, applying Re F criteria by analogy to irreversible and morally sensitive decisions.
legal_issues: Whether Re SG remains correct that court declaration is not required before abortion of incapacitated patient
Interaction of Abortion Act 1967, inherent jurisdiction and Human Rights Act 1998
When termination cases are sufficiently 'special' to require court involvement

enrichment.short_title: Director personally liable under Insolvency Act s217 where successor company name 'Air Equipment' suggested association with liquidated 'Air Component'
key_facts: Air Component Company Ltd went into creditors' voluntary liquidation on 10 February 1998; Mr Ricketts was a director from 2 January 1998.
From 2 March 1998 Ricketts was director of Air Equipment Company Ltd, renamed from Getseen Ltd in December 1997, without court leave under s216.
Ad Valorem Factors, assignee of a £6,596 debt owed by Air Equipment, obtained summary judgment holding Ricketts personally liable under s217.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Leapfrog appeal to Court of Appeal (CPR Part 52.14) from summary judgment in Redditch County Court.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; name held prohibited; personal liability upheld; permission to appeal to House of Lords refused.
enrichment.ratio: Section 216(2)(b) requires only that a name be so similar as to suggest an association with the liquidating company, not that anyone was actually misled; the provision applies beyond classic phoenix fraud cases and directors must seek court leave or resign to avoid criminal and civil liability.
legal_issues: Whether 'Air Equipment Company Limited' was a prohibited name similar to 'The Air Component Company Limited'
Purposive construction and phoenix syndrome policy
Whether similarity threshold requires actual deception
Application to associated group companies and Rule 4.230 exception

enrichment.short_title: Murder convictions at Holloway pub ambush upheld; Savva's VIPER identification evidence held admissible, Nugent's orchestration appeal dismissed
key_facts: On 16 June 2000 Mr Thomas was killed and Mr Shillibeer seriously wounded in orchestrated attacks outside The Litten Tree, Holloway Road, following an earlier altercation with Nugent and Oti.
Savva and Nugent were convicted of murder and wounding with intent; co-defendant Oti was acquitted.
Savva challenged VIPER video identification after police declined a conventional parade; Nugent challenged no-case-to-answer, summing-up and inconsistent verdicts with Oti's acquittal.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal against conviction (Savva by leave; Nugent leave granted on renewal after single judge refusal).
enrichment.ratio: VIPER identification evidence may be admissible under PACE s78 despite Code D breach where the procedure was fair and the jury could assess similarities themselves; a case to answer existed where Nugent's motive, telephone use, threats and presence supported inference of organising a joint attack; acquittal of a co-defendant on different identification issues does not render remaining convictions inconsistent.
legal_issues: Admissibility of VIPER identification after failure to hold identification parade
Whether Nugent had no case to answer on joint enterprise murder
Adequacy of jury directions on encouragement and secondary participation
Whether verdicts against Nugent were inconsistent with Oti's acquittal

enrichment.short_title: Council's refusal to modify s106 open-space obligation quashed where Secretary of State had already approved encroaching five-house scheme
key_facts: Batchelor Enterprises entered a s106 agreement in July 1999 to maintain a grassed open area at Oakcrest Service Station, Charlton Marshall, as a condition of five-house planning permission.

After construction began, access B across the forecourt was discovered to be a public highway; the Secretary of State allowed an appeal for a revised five-house scheme requiring a new access encroaching on the protected grassed area.
North Dorset District Council refused the developer's request under s106A(1)(a) to modify the obligation, citing public interest in preserving the open space.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Application for judicial review of Development Control Committee decision refusing to agree modification within the five-year s106A period.
enrichment.outcome: Application allowed; committee decision quashed as Wednesbury unreasonable; costs awarded.
enrichment.ratio: A local planning authority's discretion under s106A(1)(a) must be exercised for planning purposes; where the Secretary of State has rejected the same amenity objections on appeal, it is unreasonable for the authority to maintain its original view without explaining why the obligation still serves a useful planning purpose, especially when s106B appeal would likely succeed after the five-year period.
legal_issues: Scope of discretion under s106A(1)(a) before expiry of five-year period
Whether obligation must still serve a useful planning purpose
Effect of Secretary of State appeal decision on council's modification request
Application of Circular 1/97 paragraph C4 five-year policy

enrichment.short_title: Five wounding-with-intent convictions at Caversham wedding violence upheld; life sentence minimum term reduced to 4 years 2 months
key_facts: On 23 June 2001 at a Holiday Inn, Caversham wedding reception, members of the Rooney and Stevens/Collins travelling families fought violently for 20-30 minutes.
Stevens was convicted of five counts of wounding with intent against Rooney family members; co-accused Collins was convicted on one count.

Identification relied on VIPER video procedure after police decided a conventional parade was impracticable; Stevens was sentenced to life with an initial 12-year tariff including activated suspended sentence.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal against conviction and sentence by leave of the single judge in the Court of Appeal (Criminal Division).
enrichment.outcome: Conviction appeal dismissed; sentence appeal allowed in part—minimum term corrected to 4 years 2 months after deducting time on remand from 5-year tariff.
enrichment.ratio: VIPER identification evidence may be admitted under PACE s78 despite Code D breach where the procedure was fair; for life sentences the tariff for the index offences must be set without treating an unrelated activated suspended sentence as an associated offence under s82A(3), though the suspended sentence runs concurrently.
legal_issues: Admissibility of VIPER identification after Code D breach
Fairness of video procedure where suspect had neck scar
Whether summing-up improperly bolstered VIPER reliability
Correct calculation of life sentence minimum term with activated suspended sentence
